items.followUp: State four characteristics of a true solution.

rubric.why: A suspension is a heterogeneous mixture.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the mixture is heterogeneous or has different phases.

rubric.why: Suspended particles are large enough to be seen.
rubric.description: Mentions the visibility or relatively large size of the particles.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the particles are visible or large.

rubric.why: Suspended particles settle when the mixture is left undisturbed.
rubric.description: States that particles settle on standing.
rubric.how: Award for describing settling or sedimentation.

rubric.why: The suspended particles can be separated from the mixture by filtration.
rubric.description: States that a suspension can be separated by filtration.
rubric.how: Award for naming filtration as a separation method.

modelAnswer: A suspension is a heterogeneous mixture.
Its particles are large enough to be seen.
The particles settle down when the mixture is left undisturbed.
The particles can be separated from the mixture by filtration.

items.followUp: Define a compound and state the significance of its chemical formula.

rubric.why: An element contains only one kind of atom.
rubric.description: Defines an element as a pure substance made of one kind of atom.
rubric.how: Award for stating that an element consists of the same type of atoms.

rubric.why: An element's symbol represents one atom and can indicate its atomic mass in atomic mass units.
rubric.description: Explains the significance of an element's symbol.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the symbol represents one atom, its atomic mass, or both.

modelAnswer: An element is a pure substance made up of only one kind of atom.
The symbol of an element represents one atom of that element and also indicates its atomic mass in atomic mass units.

items.followUp: How many particles are present in one mole of a substance? Give an example.

rubric.why: One mole contains Avogadro's number of elementary entities.
rubric.description: Defines a mole using Avogadro's number.
rubric.how: Award for stating that one mole contains approximately 6.02 × 10²³ entities.

rubric.why: A valid example connects one mole with a specified number or amount of particles.
rubric.description: Gives an example of one mole.
rubric.how: Award for an example such as 1 mol of carbon atoms containing 6.02 × 10²³ atoms, or 12 g of carbon-12.

modelAnswer: One mole is the amount of a substance that contains 6.02 × 10²³ elementary entities.
For example, 1 mol of carbon atoms contains 6.02 × 10²³ carbon atoms (12 g of carbon-12).

items.followUp: Describe how Goldstein observed canal rays in a discharge tube.

rubric.why: The observation involved a gas discharge tube with a perforated cathode.
rubric.description: States the apparatus or setup used to observe the positive rays.
rubric.how: Award for mentioning a discharge tube and its perforated cathode.

rubric.why: The rays passing through the cathode holes were positive; the hydrogen nucleus was later identified as the proton.
rubric.description: States what was observed or how the proton was identified.
rubric.how: Award for identifying canal/positive rays, or stating that the hydrogen nucleus was identified as the proton.

modelAnswer: In 1886, Goldstein used a gas discharge tube containing a perforated cathode.
He observed rays passing through the holes in the cathode; these were called canal rays and consisted of positively charged particles.
The hydrogen nucleus was later identified as the proton.

items.followUp: Write the electronic configuration of a chlorine atom, atomic number 17, in shells.

rubric.why: Phosphorus has 15 electrons arranged as 2 in the first shell, 8 in the second, and 5 in the third.
rubric.description: Gives the correct shell electronic configuration for phosphorus.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for 2, 8, 5; award 1 mark if one shell count is incorrect but the distribution totals 15 electrons.

modelAnswer: Phosphorus has atomic number 15, so a neutral phosphorus atom has 15 electrons.

items.followUp: How many groups and periods are present in the modern periodic table?

rubric.why: Groups are the vertical columns of the periodic table.
rubric.how: Award for describing groups as vertical columns.

rubric.why: Periods are the horizontal rows of the periodic table.
rubric.how: Award for describing periods as horizontal rows.

modelAnswer: Groups are the vertical columns of the periodic table.
Periods are the horizontal rows of the periodic table.

items.followUp: Define ionization energy and give an example of an atom forming a positive ion.

rubric.why: Electron affinity is associated with energy released when an atom accepts an electron.
rubric.description: States that energy is released when an electron is accepted.
rubric.how: Award for mentioning release or liberation of energy.

rubric.why: The definition applies to an isolated gaseous neutral atom accepting an electron to form a negative ion.
rubric.description: Identifies the gaseous atom and provides an example of electron acceptance.
rubric.how: Award for specifying a gaseous atom forming an anion, with a valid example such as Cl + e → Cl⁻.

modelAnswer: Electron affinity is the energy released when a neutral gaseous atom accepts an electron to form a negative ion.
For example: Cl(g) + e⁻ → Cl⁻(g) + energy.

items.followUp: Define a single covalent bond and give an example.

rubric.why: A double covalent bond involves two shared pairs of electrons.
rubric.description: States the number of shared electron pairs in a double bond.
rubric.how: Award for stating that two pairs, or four electrons, are shared.

rubric.why: A correct example demonstrates a double covalent bond.
rubric.description: Gives a valid example of a double covalent bond.
rubric.how: Award for an example such as O₂ (O=O) or a C=O bond in CO₂.

modelAnswer: A double covalent bond is formed when two atoms share two pairs of electrons.
For example, the two oxygen atoms in an oxygen molecule share two pairs of electrons: O=O.
